Without a pre-publication review period, Recipient could publish results that inadvertently disclose St. Jude's proprietary information or jeopardize patent filings. Standard MTA practice includes a 30–60 day review period for the provider to review manuscripts and request removal of confidential information or delay publication to allow patent filings.

issues.title: Grant-Back License Too Narrow for St. Jude
issues.description: Section 8  grants St. Jude only a "non-exclusive, royalty-free license to use for non-commercial purposes" inventions arising from use of the Material. Given that St. Jude is providing its proprietary Material, this grant-back is quite limited. St. Jude should negotiate for at least a non-exclusive, royalty-free license for all purposes (including commercial), or alternatively secure an option to negotiate a commercial license. Without broader rights, Recipient could develop commercially valuable inventions based on St. Jude's proprietary construct and St. Jude would have no path to commercial use of those downstream inventions.

issues.description: Clause 7  requires Recipient to "destroy all unused Materials" upon termination. This obligation is problematic because: (1) there is no wind-down period allowing UPenn to complete ongoing experiments; (2) there is no carve-out for Materials already incorporated into derivatives or products; and (3) there is no exception for Materials that must be retained for regulatory or legal compliance. UPenn should negotiate a reasonable wind-down period and appropriate carve-outs.

issues.comment: We modified the destruction obligation to include a 60-day wind-down period and limited carve-outs for regulatory compliance and ongoing experiments, which reflects standard academic research practice and avoids placing UPenn in breach of applicable regulatory retention requirements.

issues.title: Short Termination Notice Period With No Cause Requirement
issues.description: Clause 7  allows either party to terminate on just 30 days' written notice, with no cause required. While mutual termination-for-convenience is common, a 30-day window is short for a research collaboration — UPenn may have committed significant resources and time. Consider extending to 60 or 90 days to allow orderly wind-down of research activities.

issues.comment: A 30-day termination notice period is unusually short for a research collaboration where both parties commit significant resources; a longer notice period ensures orderly wind-down and is consistent with standard practice in sponsored research agreements.

issues.title: No IP Ownership Provision for UPenn Inventions
issues.description: Clause 8 addresses patent filing rights and grant-back licenses but never explicitly confirms that UPenn owns inventions made solely by its researchers. While UPenn's right to file patents is mentioned , the clause should affirmatively state that inventions conceived solely by Recipient Scientist belong to UPenn, and joint inventions are jointly owned — consistent with standard academic collaboration practice. The current ambiguity, combined with the broad "Material" definition, could be used by St. Jude to claim ownership of UPenn-developed innovations.

issues.comment: We clarified IP ownership to reflect standard academic collaboration norms: solely-conceived inventions vest in the inventing party, and joint inventions are jointly owned — this resolves ambiguity that could otherwise lead to disputed ownership claims.

issues.title: No Restriction on Material Transfer Prevents Exclusivity
issues.description: Clause 5  expressly reserves St. Jude's "unrestricted right to distribute the Material to other commercial or noncommercial entities." While this is standard for basic MTAs, this is styled as a "Collaboration" agreement. The unrestricted right to share the Material with competitors — including commercial entities — could undermine UPenn's research advantage and any IP position developed through the collaboration. UPenn should consider negotiating at minimum a notice requirement, or a limited exclusivity period for the specific field of use.

issues.comment: We revised the distribution provision to restrict commercial transfers and require prior written notice, as unrestricted commercial distribution to third parties is inconsistent with the collaborative nature of this agreement and could undermine the Recipient's legitimate interest in protecting its research position.

issues.description: Clause 6  provides for joint publication "in accordance with academic standards" but does not include any pre-publication review period. This is a significant gap — without a review period, either party could inadvertently publish results that would destroy patentability of the other's inventions. UPenn should add a standard 30-day review right before any publication, allowing either party to delay publication to file patent applications.

issues.title: 60-Day Patent Filing Notification Deadline Is Short
issues.description: Clause 8  requires UPenn to notify St. Jude within 60 days of filing any patent application claiming subject matter containing the Material. This is a relatively tight deadline for a university technology licensing office. Missing this deadline could be characterized as a breach. UPenn should negotiate a longer notification window (e.g., 90 or 120 days) or clarify that failure to notify within the period is not a material breach.

issues.title: No Surviving Obligations After Termination
issues.description: Clause 7  addresses termination but does not specify which obligations survive termination. Key provisions that should survive include: the warranty disclaimer (Clause 9), liability provisions (Clause 10), the grant-back license (Clause 8), IP ownership, and publication rights. Without a survival clause, there is uncertainty about the parties' post-termination rights and obligations.

issues.title: No Human Use Prohibition May Conflict With Future Clinical Plans
issues.description: Clause 4  flatly prohibits the Material from being "used in humans." Combined with the pre-clinical-only restriction in Clause 3, this creates a hard barrier to any future clinical translation. If UPenn's collaborative research yields promising results, it would need to negotiate an entirely new agreement before any clinical use. UPenn should consider adding language that allows the parties to negotiate in good faith an amendment permitting clinical use upon completion of successful pre-clinical studies.
